issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
issues.explanation: For a 56-year-old combat pilot whose index trauma is a life-threatening accident, the trigger set is dominated by bodily-state cues (dizziness, feeling ill), which fits accident-related threat. 'Other people expressing anger, even calmly' points instead toward an interpersonal/assault schema and is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, especially given the absence of other social-conflict or perpetrator-related items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies pervasive interpersonal mistrust. In this profile, the appraisals otherwise center on emotional deadness and a shattered worldview after accident trauma. Strong distrust of others is possible, but here it lacks support from the trigger/threat/memory pattern and feels mismatched with a non-interpersonal accident presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm' conflicts with the rest of the threat profile, which is strongly hypervigilant and danger-sensitive (body on alert, startle to movement) and with avoidance-based coping. While some trauma survivors do engage in risk taking, this specific item sits awkwardly in a profile otherwise organized around fear, somatic triggering, and withdrawal, without corroborating disinhibition or anger-driven strategies.

vignette: Thomas Vance was seventy thousand feet above the desert when the right engine catastrophically failed. The subsequent explosion tore through the fuselage, and the violent deceleration sent his vision swimming with a nauseating dizziness that left him feeling utterly ill. He wrestled the aircraft through the final descent, the metallic cracks of the landing gear embedding themselves in his nervous system. When he finally walked away from the crumpled fuselage, the world no longer felt like a domain of calculated precision; it felt fundamentally treacherous. Over the next several months, the memory of that descent did not fade but recalibrated his senses. Whenever he heard a car backfire or a heavy door slam at the flight line, the familiar wave of dizziness would return, accompanied by a visceral feeling of being physically unwell. These sensory shocks immediately locked his shoulders tight and sent his entire body into a state of constant readiness to react. He found himself scanning every briefing room and aircraft hangar for threats, his eyes darting to shadows and every sudden shift in posture triggering a violent flinch. Thomas began to interpret these reactions not as normal stress responses, but as proof that his own mind was fracturing. He felt completely dead inside, a hollowed-out shell where his former confidence used to reside, and he became certain that the rigid laws of safety and control he had once trusted were completely shattered. Fearing another physical collapse, Thomas adopted rigid routines to stabilize himself. He stopped attending squadron socials or weekend trips, telling himself he simply lacked the energy, when the truth was he was giving up all pleasant activities to conserve control. He began strictly rationing his meals, measuring every portion, because regulating his stomach felt like the only way to prevent another bout of dizziness. This relentless self-policing, however, only deepened his conviction that he was fundamentally broken. He viewed his own reactions as evidence that he could not trust his own body to keep him safe, and he avoided hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations as if they were death sentences. The stricter he became about these restrictions, the more certain he became that he was irreparably damaged. In turn, this profound sense of internal and external threat kept his attention permanently fixed on danger. The moment he noticed a drop in the barometer or heard a distant thud, his body would immediately flood with tension, and his startle response would fire before his conscious mind could even process the sound. Thomas knew he was in a trap. The very act of isolation convinced him that the world was inherently dangerous, which only made him more watchful and more prone to dizziness at the slightest provocation. Now, at fifty-six, Thomas sits in a ground operations office, the hum of the ventilation system feeling unnervingly like an engine turning over. The weight of his own vigilance has grown unbearable, and the strain on his marriage has reached a breaking point; his wife no longer knows how to reach him without triggering a startle response. He has finally walked into a clinic, not because he expects a quick fix, but because he is terrified that one more explosion of sound, one more dizzy spell, will cost him his family or his license entirely. He hopes, quietly, to learn how to stand still in his own life again.
